analysis.title: Global Strategy Weekly: As the bond market bares its teeth, it's not a good time to be swimming naked
key_insights: Albert Edwards notes 10y French bond yields have risen above 5% on concern that recent riots in France worsen the fiscal arithmetic. He asks whether the 2026 global bond bear market is driven by macro fundamentals or by a downturn in the global liquidity cycle, and whether equities are next.

Edwards agrees with Larry Jeddeloh of The Institutional Strategist that bonds are in a long secular bear market, a mirror image of the 1980-2020 secular descent in yields. Jeddeloh's 10% US 10y target is for a couple of cycles out, not this cycle.

Edwards compares this to Ray Dalio's view that investors will be surprised by how high rates must go, not in the current cycle but in the next one. He says clients are being told 5% yields are the old normal after the QE/ZIRP bond bubble.

Edwards and Ed Ballsdon (The Grey Fire Horse) argue the key fiscal vulnerability metric is government interest payments as a ratio to government revenues, not GDP. Dalio highlighted the same ratio for the US a week after Ballsdon's 6 October piece.

Edwards names the UK, France, the US and China as the four biggest fiscal offenders. He says China needs including and that its current primary deficit is very large. He contrasts this with the late 1990s tech bubble, when governments ran large primary and overall surpluses.

Government net interest payments are close to 4% of GDP in the US and rising rapidly to 3% in France. On interest payments as a share of revenues, the US is in a much worse position than the others, especially on Ballsdon's extrapolations.

Dalio says US debt burdens (interest and total debt service as a share of revenue) are at their highest since WWII and expected to worsen. He sees the US debt roll-over as crucial if global liquidity is becoming an issue.

SG Rates research (Ninon Bachet and Mathias Kpade) says the UK and Japan look relatively safe on roll-over vulnerability, while the US does not. The UK gilt market is especially exposed to higher inflation, per the OBR, so the UK cannot inflate its way out of debt.

The OECD and SG Rates note the investor base for major bond markets has shifted toward more fickle buyers. France is most at risk on this measure and Japan least. The IMF Investor Risk Index has risen across most major sovereigns since 2023, with France and Italy combining high debt with weaker investor bases.

In IMF shock scenarios, debt-to-GDP in 2028 rises in every case for the US, from a 131.3 baseline to 135.1 under a growth/inflation -1pp shock. France's trajectory rises in most scenarios, while the UK's levels out or falls.

SG Rates doubts the IMF's French path because it assumes a meaningful primary balance improvement amid political uncertainty. Using SG economists' primary balance forecasts gives a significantly steeper French debt trajectory, especially with weaker growth or fiscal slippage.

Edwards asks whether receding excess liquidity matters more than macro fundamentals for bonds and equities. He cites David Howell of CrossBorder Capital, who warns the excess liquidity tide is going out, and presents a chart arguing China's credit impulse leads the US equity market lower.
